items.text: Turn students' strong passive understanding of home (colloquial Jakarta-style) Indonesian into confident, accurate speaking, reading and writing.
Give students control of both registers: everyday informal Indonesian and standard/formal Indonesian (bahasa baku), and the judgement to choose between them.
Build a large, active vocabulary (about 1,800 core items taught explicitly, plus personal and incidental vocabulary) organised by word family and affix.
Master the core morphology of Indonesian – especially affixation – which is the main gap for heritage learners.
Reach CEFR B2 overall by the end of Year 2 (listening likely higher), with evidence recorded against CEFR can-do descriptors and the Indonesian BIPA competency levels.
Deepen students' connection to Indonesian culture, history and literature, and to their own bilingual, bicultural identity.

rows.text: 2 school years; 40 teaching weeks per year in 4 terms of 10 weeks (8 terms in total).
1 lesson of about 60 minutes per day, 5 days a week = 50 lessons per term, 200 per year, about 400 hours in total.
Weeks 1–8: four 2-week thematic units. Week 9: project week. Week 10: assessment, feedback and consolidation.
About 15 minutes of spaced-repetition review a day plus 60 minutes a week of extensive reading or listening, and one short weekly family task (about 2 hours a week in total).
Teenagers (about 13–17) with one Indonesian-speaking parent; they understand everyday home Indonesian but speak, read and write it weakly. Class size assumed to be 10–20.

Uneven profile, typical of heritage learners: listening roughly A2+/B1 for familiar everyday topics; speaking A1–A2 (often mixed with English); reading and writing A1–A2; little control of formal register or affixes.
A school in Indonesia, so authentic input and real-world tasks (markets, transport, local community, news) are all around the students.
Teacher-curated authentic materials plus the free Badan Bahasa BIPA series Sahabatku Indonesia untuk Pelajar (BIPA 1–7) as a reference spine.

runs.text: Why start at A2 and not A1? Heritage learners already know the sound system, basic word order, a few thousand receptive words and a lot of everyday chunks. Starting at A1 would waste their advantage and bore them. Term 1 therefore consolidates A2 production quickly, while listening and reading input is pitched higher (B1) from the start.

Why aim for B2 and not C1? About 400 contact hours plus about 150 hours of structured independent study, on top of a strong receptive base and daily exposure in Indonesia, makes B2 (independent user: can discuss abstract topics, argue a view, and write clear, detailed formal texts) ambitious but realistic. C1 needs sustained academic reading and writing that goes beyond a 5-lesson-a-week school course; able students can still reach C1 in listening.

Why CEFR? It is the international reference for language levels, it has detailed can-do descriptors for teenagers' communicative tasks (updated in the 2020 Companion Volume, including mediation), and Indonesia's own BIPA competency standards (Permendikbud No. 27 Tahun 2017, 7 levels) were explicitly adapted from CEFR. So the CEFR spine lines up with Indonesian national materials.
Indicative alignment used for planning (not an official equivalence): Terms 1–2 ≈ BIPA 2 (A2), Terms 3–4 ≈ BIPA 3 (B1), Terms 5–6 ≈ BIPA 4 (B1+), Terms 7–8 ≈ BIPA 5 (B2).

home.text: 1.4 Methods and how each is used

headers: How it is used in this course

rows.text: The progression spine. Each term has a CEFR target and 'can-do' statements that drive the task design, the rubrics and student self-assessment.
Information gaps, role-plays (warung, market, clinic, job interview), surveys and discussions every week; accuracy is taught in service of communication.
Every Wednesday runs a pre-task → task → planning → report → language-focus cycle. Week 9 of every term is a larger project (e.g. class news bulletin, debate tournament, cultural evening).

Monday input lessons use stories, songs, video, news and texts slightly above current level. Because heritage students understand more than they can say, input is pitched about half a level above the output target. Themes are recycled over two weeks ('narrow input') so that vocabulary repeats naturally.

Start from what students already know (home Indonesian), make it explicit, then bridge it to standard forms: colloquial → baku mapping tables, register-switch rewriting, and literacy through genres they meet in real life. The home variety is valued, not 'corrected away'. Weekly family tasks (e.g. interview a parent) turn home into a source of input and output. Targets typical gaps: affixes, formal pronouns and address, spelling (EYD), and extended talk.

Tuesday lessons draw grammar from Monday's text (noticing), explain it briefly and explicitly, then move from controlled to freer practice. There is a planned sequence for affixation (ber-, meN-, di-, ter-, -kan, -i, ke-…-an, peN-, peN-…-an, per-…-an, memper-), reduplication, aspect markers, classifiers and register.

Each term's vocabulary list is issued as an Anki deck (recognition, production, cloze-sentence and audio cards). About 5–8 new list cards per school day plus personal words from reading. Time is balanced across Nation's four strands: meaning-focused input, meaning-focused output, language-focused learning and fluency development.

Pronoun and address systems (saya/aku/gue; Anda/kamu/lu; Bapak/Ibu/Kak) are taught from week 1. Speaking tasks state the required register; written tasks use baku unless the genre is informal (chat, social media).
Comprehensible input on the unit theme (text, video, song, story); new words met in context; word-family mapping; new SRS cards released.
Noticing the target structure in Monday's input; short explicit explanation (usually an affix or aspect/register point); controlled → freer practice; mini-quiz on the exit ticket.
Task cycle: pre-task, pair or group task, planning, report to class, feedback and language focus. The register is set by the task.
Authentic text of the target genre; genre and structure analysis; guided writing; colloquial → baku rewriting; peer editing using EYD checklists.
Vocabulary and grammar quiz (15 min); fluency games; extensive reading/listening time; reflection against can-do statements; weekend family task set.

runs.text: A typical 60-minute lesson: warm-up and SRS check (5–10 min) → main input or task (35–40 min) → consolidation and error focus (10 min) → exit ticket (5 min).

Each 10-week term follows the same shape: four 2-week units (weeks 1–8), a project week (week 9) in which students use the term's language in an extended task, and an assessment and consolidation week (week 10).

items.text: About 1,800 core words and phrases are listed in Section 3, rising from about 205 in Term 1 to about 250 in Term 8 (Year 1 ≈ 850, Year 2 ≈ 965). The lists are a minimum: students also add personal words from their reading and from home.
Words are grouped by theme and taught as families (e.g. makan → makanan, memakan, dimakan), so every affix lesson also grows vocabulary.
Colloquial items are marked [coll.] with the standard form after '→'. Heritage students usually know the colloquial form; the goal is to add the standard one, not to replace the home one.
Spelling follows EYD Edition V and KBBI (e.g. Idulfitri, salat, kaus, antre, karier, apotek, utang).

runs.text: Colloquial Indonesian is the students' strength and the language of their homes; it is used as the starting point, not treated as an error. Every task states its register. In speaking tasks with peers, natural informal Indonesian is welcome; in presentations, interviews and all formal writing, standard Indonesian (bahasa baku) is required and assessed. Appendix A sets out the pronoun system and the main colloquial Jakarta features, with their standard equivalents.

Each term lists its CEFR target, themes, grammar, speaking and writing tasks, authentic materials and assessment, followed by a week-by-week outline. Grammar is cumulative: earlier points are recycled in later terms.

terms.title: Term 1: Aku dan Duniaku (Me and my world)

runs.text: CEFR target:
A2 production (consolidation); input pitched at B1 · ≈ BIPA 2
Activate what students already understand, get them talking from day one, and make the register system explicit.

rows.text: Identity and introductions; family and home languages; school life; daily routine and time; describing people.
• Basic clause structure: subject–verb–object, noun + adjective, relative marker yang
• Pronouns and address terms by register: saya/aku/gue; Anda/kamu/lu; Bapak/Ibu/Kak; kami vs kita
• Aspect markers: sudah, belum, sedang, akan, masih, baru, pernah
• Question words and apakah; numbers, dates, clock time
• Colloquial → formal bridge: nggak → tidak, udah → sudah, gimana → bagaimana; first look at -in → -kan/-i
• 'Siapa aku?' partner interview, then introduce your partner to the class
• Family-tree presentation (including which languages are spoken at home)
• Same message, two registers: ask a teacher vs a friend for help
• 'A day in my life' blog post (informal)
• Register switch: rewrite a WhatsApp chat as a polite message to a teacher
• Sahabatku Indonesia untuk Pelajar BIPA 1–2 (selected units)
• Real school documents: timetables, notices, the school website
• Short 'day in my life' vlogs by Indonesian teenagers (teacher-selected)
• Students' own (anonymised) family chats as data for register work
• Week 1 diagnostic: listening, speaking interview, short writing, register awareness
• Weekly Friday vocabulary and grammar quizzes
• End of term: A2 oral interview (5 min), personal profile, listening test
• Week 1: Diagnostic; introductions; 'Who says gue?' register awareness
• Week 2: Identity and origins; pronouns and address terms
• Week 3–4: Family: family trees, descriptions, possession
• Week 5–6: School life: negation, question words, timetables
• Week 7–8: Daily routine and time: aspect markers
• Week 9: Project: 'Profil Saya' video or poster in formal and informal versions

runs.text: CEFR target:
A2 secure → A2+ · ≈ BIPA 2
Use Indonesia as the classroom: food, markets, homes and friends, with meN- verbs as the grammar centrepiece.

rows.text: Food and eating out; shopping and money; home and chores; friends and hobbies; weather.
• meN- verbs and nasal assimilation (membaca, menulis, menyapu, mengirim, memasak)
• ber- vs meN-: intransitive vs transitive (bermain vs memainkan preview)
• Classifiers with se-: seorang, sebuah, seekor, selembar, sebiji, sebatang, sepotong
• Plurals: reduplication (buku-buku) and quantifiers (banyak, beberapa, semua)
• Comparison: lebih … daripada, paling, ter- superlative, se- equative
• Requests and commands: tolong, silakan, -lah, jangan
• Market bargaining role-play using real prices
• Ordering at a warung (and handling problems with the order)
• Hobby survey: collect data and report back
• Invitation: informal to a friend vs formal to a teacher
• Real menus from local warung and food-delivery apps (screenshots)
• Role-play (bargaining or ordering), assessed with rubric
• meN- form test; weekly quizzes; listening to shop and market dialogues
• Week 1–2: Food and eating out: meN- verbs, classifiers
• Week 3–4: Shopping and money: numbers, bargaining, comparison
• Week 5–6: Home and chores: commands and requests, -nya
• Week 7–8: Friends, hobbies, weather: ber- verbs, reduplication
• Week 9: Project: class 'warung day' or narrated cooking video

runs.text: CEFR target:
B1 (entry) · ≈ BIPA 3
Teen interests drive the input; passives, ter- and ke-…-an unlock narrative and description.

rows.text: Social media and devices; music and film; sport; body and health; feelings; appearance and personality.
• di- passive and object focus (Video itu diunggah kemarin)
• Passive type 2 with pronoun agents (Lagu itu sudah saya dengar; kubaca)
• ter-: accidental action and resultant state (tertidur, terbuka, tersesat)
• Narrative connectors: lalu, kemudian, setelah itu, waktu, walaupun, supaya
• Relative clauses with yang (lagu yang paling saya suka)
• Vlog-style review of a song or film
• Survey of classmates' social-media habits, presented with a chart
• Doctor–patient role-play at a clinic or pharmacy
• Story of a 'bad day' using ter- and ke-…-an
• Social-media post vs formal reply to a comment
• Rewrite an informal chat as a formal email
• Indonesian pop songs and lyrics (e.g. Tulus, Hindia, Nadin Amizah, Bernadya)
• Film trailers and clips (e.g. Petualangan Sherina, 2000; Keluarga Cemara, 2019)
• Health leaflets from a puskesmas; Sahabatku Indonesia untuk Pelajar BIPA 3
• Passive and affix test; song gap-fill and interview listening
• Week 1–2: Social media and devices: di- passive in signs and instructions ('Dilarang …')
• Week 3–4: Music and film: reviews, -kan and -i
• Week 5–6: Sport and fitness: passive type 2, match commentary
• Week 7–8: Body, health and feelings: ter-, ke-…-an
• Week 9: Project: class podcast (siniar) or vlog episode

runs.text: CEFR target:
B1 (secure) · ≈ BIPA 3 · end-of-Year-1 checkpoint
Travel, geography and culture, with nominal affixes and reported speech; the family becomes a research source.

rows.text: Transport and directions; travel and accommodation; geography and nature; everyday environment; festivals, religion and customs; traditional arts.
• peN- agent nouns and peN-…-an / per-…-an nouns (penumpang, perjalanan, pertemuan)
• Reported speech: katanya, bahwa, menurut, apakah
• Location and direction phrases; time clauses (sebelum, sesudah, ketika)
• Word-family work: jalan → berjalan, perjalanan, menjalankan
• Plan a trip itinerary and 'sell' it to clients
• Map task: asking for and giving directions
• Presentation on a festival, including personal and family experience
• Interview a parent about their home town (heritage task)
• Report of the parent interview using reported speech
• Official tourism material (e.g. the Wonderful Indonesia campaign)
• Train and ferry timetables, maps, ride-hailing app screens
• Folk legends (e.g. Malin Kundang, Danau Toba)
• Laskar Pelangi (film, 2008) excerpts set in Belitung; Sahabatku Indonesia untuk Pelajar BIPA 3
• B1 oral presentation with Q&A (province or festival)
• B1 writing: descriptive or narrative text (300 words)
• Year-end listening and reading test; portfolio review; SRS statistics
• Week 3–4: Geography and nature: each student adopts a province
• Week 5–6: Festivals, religion, customs; gotong royong
• Week 7–8: Heritage project: interviewing parents; reported speech
• Week 10: End-of-Year-1 assessment and CEFR checkpoint

runs.text: CEFR target:
B1+ · ≈ BIPA 4
Move into the public, formal register through news, society and technology.

rows.text: News and media literacy; government, elections and community; science and technology; digital life and online safety; disasters and emergencies.
• Nominalisation in news style (pembangunan, kemiskinan, penemuan); headline style
• Formal connectors: namun, oleh karena itu, sehingga, selain itu, adapun
• Produce and perform a 5-minute news bulletin
• Interview a community figure (e.g. head of RT, school staff member)
• Structured discussion of a current news story
• News report (5W + 1H: apa, siapa, kapan, di mana, mengapa, bagaimana)
• Formal letter to a local authority about a community issue
• Kompas, Tempo, BBC News Indonesia, detikcom
• TV news clips (e.g. Kompas TV, Metro TV); Narasi programmes
• BMKG public warnings; Kok Bisa? science explainer videos
• News bulletin performance (group and individual marks)
• Authentic news reading test; memper-/-kan/-i test
• Week 1–2: News and media literacy: news-report genre
• Week 5–6: Science, technology and digital life (hoaxes, digital footprint)
• Week 7–8: Disasters and emergencies (early warning, response)

runs.text: CEFR target:
B1+ → B2 (developing) · ≈ BIPA 4
Argue, persuade and negotiate on issues teenagers care about.

rows.text: Opinion and debate; social issues and youth; environment and climate; health and wellbeing; education and urban issues.
• Argumentative text structure: thesis – arguments – reaffirmation
• Conditionals: jika, apabila, seandainya, andaikan, kalau saja
• Concession and contrast: meskipun, biarpun, padahal, sebaliknya
• Modality and hedging: seharusnya, sebaiknya, boleh jadi, belum tentu, tampaknya
• Reduplication with affixes: tolong-menolong, secepat-cepatnya, kebarat-baratan
• Cause and effect: menyebabkan, mengakibatkan, sehingga
• Structured team debates (three speakers per side) on teen-relevant motions
• Negotiation role-play (e.g. school rules, class budget)
• Opinion column or letter to the editor
• Opinion columns (Kompas, Tempo); talk-show clips (e.g. Mata Najwa)
• Infographics and data from BPS (Statistics Indonesia)
• Talk-show listening test; mid-Year-2 CEFR checkpoint (B1+)
• Week 3–4: Social issues and youth (mental health, peer pressure, gender)
• Week 5–6: Environment and climate in Indonesia (haze, deforestation, subsidence)
• Week 7–8: Education and urban issues; negotiation

runs.text: CEFR target:
B2 (entry) · ≈ BIPA 5
Formal, professional and academic Indonesian for work and study.

rows.text: Work and careers; professions; education and university; economy and business; personal finance; formal letters; academic and science language.
• Effective sentences (kalimat efektif) and formal register
• Formal passives and agentive oleh; clauses with bahwa and yang
• Letter and email conventions; hedging in reports
• Business pitch for a small-business (UMKM) product
• Mini research report (background, method, results, discussion, conclusion)
• BPS data; company profiles; Kok Bisa? videos
• Week 1–2: Jobs, careers and the workplace
• Week 3–4: Applications: CV, cover letter, interviews
• Week 5–6: Economy, business and entrepreneurship (UMKM pitch)
• Week 7–8: Academic language and mini research project (survey)
• Week 9: Project: 'Expo Karier' pitches and research presentations

terms.title: Term 8: Sejarah, Sastra, dan Jati Diri (History, literature and identity)

runs.text: CEFR target:
B2 (secure) · ≈ BIPA 5 · exit checkpoint
Read Indonesia's story and literature, reflect on identity, and bring the whole affix system together.

rows.text: Kingdoms, trade and colonialism; national awakening and independence; modern Indonesia; poetry, pantun, short stories and novels; language and identity; idioms and proverbs.
• Literary and elevated style; archaic and literary vocabulary
• Particles -lah, -kah, pun; focus with adalah, merupakan, ialah
• Historical presentation or role-play (e.g. Sumpah Pemuda 1928, Proklamasi 1945)
• Book talk on a novel extract; final oral examination
• Literary analysis of a short story (intrinsic elements)
• Original pantun and a short poem
• Reflective essay: 'Bahasa dan jati diriku' (language and my identity)
• Texts of the Sumpah Pemuda and the Proclamation of Independence
• Museum visit (e.g. Museum Nasional, or a local museum)
• Extracts from Laskar Pelangi (Andrea Hirata) and Bumi Manusia (Pramoedya Ananta Toer; film 2019)
• Poems by Chairil Anwar and Sapardi Djoko Damono; folk tales (Malin Kundang, Sangkuriang, Timun Mas); Sunday short stories in Kompas
• Final examination in all four skills
• Final oral; portfolio review; exit CEFR checkpoint (B2)
• Week 1–2: Kingdoms, spice trade and colonial rule
• Week 3–4: National awakening, independence, Old Order, New Order, Reformasi
• Week 5–6: Literature: poetry, pantun, short stories
• Week 7: Novel and film: Laskar Pelangi / Bumi Manusia extracts
• Week 8: Language and identity; idioms and proverbs; exam preparation
• Week 9: Project: 'Malam Budaya' literary and cultural evening
• Week 10: Final assessment and exit checkpoint

runs.text: The lists contain 1,817 words and phrases: Year 1 851, Year 2 966. Per term: T1 206; T2 210; T3 215; T4 220; T5 231; T6 240; T7 245; T8 250. Each item appears only once across the course; later terms recycle earlier words in new contexts.

items.text: Conventions:

[coll.] = colloquial/informal; '→' gives the standard (baku) equivalent; '(← root)' shows the root word so that students learn word families; '/' separates alternatives. Spelling follows EYD Edition V and KBBI.
Using the lists:
each term's list is loaded into a shared Anki deck with recognition, production and example-sentence cards. Introduce words through Monday input, not as bare lists; test a sample every Friday.
Diagnose first: in Term 1, week 1, each student gets a skills profile (listening, speaking, reading, writing, register awareness), because heritage profiles are uneven.
Assess what is taught: every summative task mirrors the term's project and genre, and is marked with the same analytic rubric.
Assess both registers: tasks specify formal or informal, and 'register control' is a separate criterion.

Make progress visible: students keep a portfolio (writing drafts, audio/video recordings, SRS statistics) and self-assess against can-do statements each term, following the European Language Portfolio model.
Report by skill: termly reports give a CEFR band for each of the four skills, not just one overall grade.

rows.text: Classwork, speaking tasks and family tasks
End-of-term writing task (genre of the term)

assessment.text: 4.3 Analytic rubric (4 bands: below target / approaching / at target / above target)

rows.text: Covers the task, audience and purpose; content is relevant and developed.
Breadth of vocabulary (including term lists) and variety of structures.
Grammar and especially affixation, word order and EYD spelling.
Chooses and keeps the right register; formal texts avoid colloquial forms; informal tasks sound natural.
Can describe family, school and routine in simple connected sentences; can switch between saya/aku and Anda/kamu appropriately.
Can write a short personal profile with basic connectors and correct spelling of common words.
Can handle everyday transactions (ordering, bargaining, prices) and give simple reasons and comparisons.
Can write a clear recipe, review or invitation in the right register.
Can narrate experiences and give opinions on music, film and sport with some detail.
Can write a structured review or narrative using di- passives and connectors.
Can give a prepared presentation and answer questions; can report what others said.
Can write a 300-word description or narrative and a formal enquiry email.
Can summarise and discuss news on familiar topics; can interview someone and follow up.
Can write a news report and a formal letter using nominalisation and formal connectors.
Can argue a position, rebut points and negotiate; is largely fluent on familiar issues.
Can write a coherent argumentative essay with conditionals, concession and hedging.
Can take part in a formal interview and present research clearly with some spontaneity.
Can write a CV, cover letter and short report in accurate formal Indonesian.
Can discuss abstract, cultural and literary topics fluently and adapt register to audience.
Can write a clear, detailed literary or historical text with good control of affixation.

items.text: End of Year 1 (Term 4, week 10):
B1 checkpoint in all four skills, including an oral presentation with questions and a 300-word text. Students below B1 in writing get targeted literacy support in Term 5.
Mid-Year 2 (Term 6, week 10):
B1+ checkpoint with a debate and an argumentative essay.
End of course (Term 8, week 10):
B2 exit examination: listening and reading papers using authentic texts, an extended formal writing task, and a 15-minute oral (presentation plus discussion).
Optional external benchmark:

UKBI Adaptif from Badan Bahasa (sections: listening, responding to grammar rules, reading, writing, speaking; 7 grades from Terbatas to Istimewa) for able Year 2 students who want an official certificate.
Stretch tasks and extra authentic reading for students whose receptive level is well above the class target.
Literacy clinics (phonics–spelling links, EYD) for students who speak well but write weakly.
Mixed-ability pairing: stronger speakers help with fluency; stronger writers help with accuracy and formal register.
Personalised Anki cards for recurring individual errors, especially affix choice.

l, m, n, ny, ng, r, w, y

runs.text: The same sound changes apply to peN- (penulis, pembaca, pengirim, penyapu). Many loan words keep their first consonant (mengkritik, mengklaim).
